title: Dutch resist ‘unacceptable’ US bid to tighten semiconductor export controls
byline: Carlo Martuscelli, Camille Gijs, Pieter Haeck
excerpt: The bipartisan MATCH Act would tighten restrictions on ASML’s sales to China, drawing objections from The Hague.

The bipartisan MATCH Act would tighten restrictions on ASML’s sales to China, drawing objections from The Hague.

November 17, 2026 7:18 pm CET

BRUSSELS — The Netherlands has pushed back against a U.S. congressional bid to tighten restrictions on exports of advanced chipmaking equipment to China, warning that Washington’s attempt to dictate the rules for Dutch companies such as ASML is unacceptable.

The Dutch objections come as the proposed MATCH Act gains fresh momentum in Washington following revelations about Nvidia’s former chief executive Jensen Huang and his links to a suspected Chinese spy, intensifying concerns in Congress about Beijing’s access to advanced U.S. technology.

The bipartisan legislation would give U.S. allies, including the Netherlands and Japan, 150 days to align restrictions on sales and servicing of advanced chipmaking equipment to China with those imposed by Washington, or show progress toward doing so. If they fail to comply, the U.S. Commerce Department would be required to extend American export controls unilaterally to equipment supplied from those countries.

“The main concern is the bill’s extraterritorial character,” a spokesperson for the Dutch Ministry of Foreign Affairs told POLITICO on Tuesday.

“The United States and the Netherlands are important partners. We maintain frequent and ongoing contact at all levels,” the Dutch spokesperson said. “Each country is responsible for its own national security policy and subsequently its export control policy. Extraterritorial measures run counter to this principle and are unacceptable between partners.”

The stakes are particularly high for ASML, the Dutch company that dominates the market for advanced lithography machines used to manufacture microchips. China accounted for nearly a third of its revenue last year, and the proposed legislation would further restrict its ability to sell and service equipment there.

The Netherlands has already imposed restrictions on exports of ASML’s chipmaking equipment to China, but has resisted U.S. efforts to go further. Prime Minister Rob Jetten raised concerns during an April visit to Washington, while Foreign Trade Minister Sjoerd Sjoerdsma took up the issue with Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and lawmakers in June.

But the dispute goes beyond commercial interests to a fundamental question of sovereignty. 

“The issue is not simply whether tighter restrictions are justified, but who defines them and through which process,” said Benedetta Girardi, a strategic analyst at the Hague Centre for Strategic Studies. “Coordinating national policies is very different from allowing one country to determine the commercial reach of companies based in another.”

The race to AI 

Europe lags the U.S. and China in the race to build advanced AI. But European companies remain critical suppliers of the hardware that powers the technology.   

The most important of these is ASML, the Dutch producer of the hyperprecise lithography machines that print patterns onto silicon wafers. The €500 billion company is the country’s biggest. Specialized machinery and parts, a category largely made up of chipmaking equipment, were the Netherlands’ second-biggest goods export in 2025.

ASML has warned that further restrictions could backfire. CFO Roger Dassen, briefing reporters on the company’s third-quarter results last month, criticized the MATCH Act and said limiting sales of chipmaking equipment to China would only accelerate the development of rival technology by competitors there.

Dutch MEP Bart Groothuis has also questioned Washington’s approach, arguing that it made little sense for the U.S. to demand tighter restrictions on European chipmaking equipment while allowing American companies to export advanced AI chips to China.

“You can’t say: they can’t have AI chips, so don’t sell them the machines, but we sell them our AI chips,” Groothuis told POLITICO last week. “It’s not right, it doesn’t make any sense.”

The impact of the MATCH Act would go beyond just ASML. Its complex machines have tens of thousands of parts, creating a dense network of suppliers that crisscrosses the globe. Germany’s ZEISS, for example, makes high-precision lenses and mirrors that direct the light used by ASML to print patterns on silicon wafers. Berlin is also among the European capitals concerned about the bill.

ASML has never shipped its most advanced extreme ultraviolet, or EUV, machines to China. The Netherlands already introduced export controls on less advanced deep ultraviolet, or DUV, machines back in 2023. The MATCH Act would expand those controls to more types of DUV chipmaking equipment and tighten rules on servicing machines already in China. 

Bernd Lange, a German MEP who chairs the European Parliament’s trade committee, said in an October interview with POLITICO that Washington’s extraterritorial approach was “totally unacceptable.” The discussion needed to happen “on equal footing,” he said.

Political push

Last week, senior lawmakers pushed to include the MATCH Act in the year-end defense bill. They also requested that Jensen Huang appear before Congress.

The scandal involving Huang has galvanized backers of the legislation, who argue that access to sensitive technology cannot be left to the whims of private business, said Hanna Dohmen, a senior research analyst at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Huang had been a leading proponent of looser export controls.

“People in Washington, in particular lawmakers, are very upset by that news,” Dohmen said.

Supporters of tighter controls argue that Beijing must be denied access to advanced chipmaking technology, and that stricter U.S. rules are pointless unless its allies are asked, or required, to follow suit.  

But critics say the revelations have also exposed contradictions in Washington’s approach. The New York Times reported that President Donald Trump was informed last fall that Huang was in a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

“There’s a lot of hypocrisy in the whole story,” said Sanne van der Lugt, co-lead of the China and Asia program at the Global Trade Policy Observatory. “If you claim to need this extraterritorial legislation for national security, you need to behave like it’s a national security issue.”

Divisions within the Trump administration could yet complicate the congressional push.

Export controls are currently largely administered by the Commerce Department, giving the White House considerable discretion. The MATCH Act would impose additional requirements through legislation, limiting that flexibility.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has come under fire for failing to blacklist Megaspeed, a company suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China. Trump has defended Lutnick, who has also faced criticism from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the lax enforcement of export controls.

The Commerce Department moved Monday to close a loophole allowing companies in restricted countries to access advanced American AI chips by renting computing power from data centers abroad. The department’s Bureau of Industry and Security said the new rule was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and National Security Council — an unusual acknowledgment that points to Lutnick being sidelined.

The scandal involving Huang has galvanized backers of the legislation, who argue that access to sensitive technology cannot be left to the whims of private business, said Hanna Dohmen, a senior research analyst at Georgetown University’s Center for Security and Emerging Technology. Huang had been a leading proponent of looser export controls.

“People in Washington, in particular lawmakers, are very upset by that news,” Dohmen said.

Supporters of tighter controls argue that Beijing must be denied access to advanced chipmaking technology, and that stricter U.S. rules are pointless unless its allies are asked, or required, to follow suit.

But critics say the revelations have also exposed contradictions in Washington’s approach. The New York Times reported that President Donald Trump was informed last fall that Huang was in a relationship with a suspected Chinese spy.

“There’s a lot of hypocrisy in the whole story,” said Sanne van der Lugt, co-lead of the China and Asia program at the Global Trade Policy Observatory. “If you claim to need this extraterritorial legislation for national security, you need to behave like it’s a national security issue.”

Divisions within the Trump administration could yet complicate the congressional push.

Export controls are currently largely administered by the Commerce Department, giving the White House considerable discretion. The MATCH Act would impose additional requirements through legislation, limiting that flexibility.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has come under fire for failing to blacklist Megaspeed, a company suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China. Trump has defended Lutnick, who has also faced criticism from Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent over the lax enforcement of export controls.

The Commerce Department moved Monday to close a loophole allowing companies in restricted countries to access advanced American AI chips by renting computing power from data centers abroad. The department’s Bureau of Industry and Security said the new rule was written by and at the direction of the Treasury Department and National Security Council — an unusual acknowledgment that points to Lutnick being sidelined.
